text.simple: Scientists pick a protein that seems to drive the disease. If you can block it, maybe you can stop the disease.
text.student: **Target identification and validation:** find a protein whose activity drives the disease (for example a stuck-on kinase), then prove that blocking it helps, often with knockdown experiments like the ones in this app. [@hughes2011]
text.deep: Targets come from genetics (driver mutations), functional genomics (CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq), and biology. Validation asks whether modulating the target changes disease-relevant phenotypes, and whether a molecule can plausibly bind it ('druggability'). [@hughes2011]

text.simple: Robots test huge libraries of chemicals to find any that stick to the target.
text.student: **Hit discovery:** high-throughput screening tests hundreds of thousands of compounds against the target. A 'hit' is any compound that has some effect. [@hughes2011]
text.deep: Hit finding uses HTS, fragment screening, DNA-encoded libraries, virtual screening, or structure-based design. Hits are usually weak (micromolar) and need confirmation in orthogonal assays. [@hughes2011]

text.simple: Chemists tweak the best chemicals again and again to make them stronger and safer.
text.student: **Lead optimization:** medicinal chemists make many variants of the best hits to improve how tightly they bind, how selective they are, and how well the body absorbs them. [@hughes2011]
text.deep: Lead optimization iterates on potency, selectivity (off-target kinases, hERG), and ADME/PK properties, often guided by co-crystal structures like the ones in this app. [@hughes2011]

text.simple: The drug is tested on cells in dishes and on animals to check that it works and is safe enough to try in people.
text.student: **Preclinical testing:** cell lines (like K562 in this app) and animal models test whether the drug works and what dose is toxic. Lots of drugs that work on cells in a dish fail later in people.
text.deep: Preclinical packages include efficacy in cell lines and xenografts or PDX models, pharmacokinetics, and GLP toxicology to support an Investigational New Drug (IND) application. Cell-line efficacy is a weak predictor of clinical benefit.

text.simple: A small group of volunteers takes the drug to check it's safe and find the right dose.
text.student: **Phase I:** usually tens of people. In cancer, often patients who have run out of other options. The main question: is it safe, and what dose?
text.deep: Phase I establishes safety, maximum tolerated or recommended phase II dose, and pharmacokinetics. Oncology phase I trials typically enroll patients with advanced disease rather than healthy volunteers.

text.simple: A bigger group tries it to see if it actually helps.
text.student: **Phase II:** often around a hundred patients or more. Does the tumor shrink? This is where many drugs fail.
text.deep: Phase II estimates efficacy (response rate, progression-free survival) and refines dosing; it has historically been the largest point of attrition.

text.simple: Hundreds or thousands of people help compare the new drug with the best treatment we already have.
text.student: **Phase III:** large trials that compare the new drug with the current standard treatment, usually by random assignment.
text.deep: Phase III randomized controlled trials test superiority or non-inferiority on clinically meaningful endpoints such as overall survival.

text.simple: Government experts check all the evidence before the drug can be sold.
text.student: **Approval:** a regulator (such as the US FDA) reviews all the data. Even after approval, safety is watched in the real world.
text.deep: Regulatory review (NDA/BLA) may use accelerated pathways for serious diseases with unmet need; post-marketing studies continue to monitor safety and confirm benefit.
